language_wrapper: On a circular track of circumference {circumference}, there are {n_points} equally spaced marked points. They are labeled A_1, A_2, ..., A_{n_points} in some order, each label used exactly once. Bunbun starts at A_1, hops to A_2, then A_3, ..., then A_{n_points}, and finally back to A_1. Every hop is along the shorter arc between the two points (if the chord is a diameter, any semicircle may be used). Over all possible labelings, determine the maximal possible value of the sum of the {power}-th powers of the lengths of the {n_points} arcs that Bunbun traverses.
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Choose n_points sufficiently large to avoid trivial cases and to ensure difficulty
    # Ensure circumference is a multiple of n_points so arc lengths are integral multiples of a unit step
    # Choose power >= 2 to make it strictly harder than the seed (which corresponds to power=1)
    for _ in range(100):
        n = rng.randint(8, 2000)  # larger than seed's logic but still manageable
        t = rng.randint(1, 20)    # step size multiplier so circumference = n * t
        C = n * t
        p = rng.choice([2, 3, 4, 5])
        # Domain checks
        if n >= 8 and C > 0 and C % n == 0 and p >= 2:
            return {'n_points': n, 'circumference': C, 'power': p}
    # Fallback deterministic assignment if random attempts somehow fail
    n = 12
    t = 3
    C = n * t
    p = 3
    return {'n_points': n, 'circumference': C, 'power': p}
hardness_rationale: The seed asks for a maximal sum of arc lengths (a linear objective). This family instead asks for the maximal sum of power-th powers of arc lengths, with power >= 2. Optimizing a convex objective under cyclic wrap constraints is significantly harder: one must reason about extreme distributions and use majorization/Karamata or equivalent convexity arguments, not just simple parity or diameter counting. The even-n case requires a delicate analysis that enforces a specific multiset of step-lengths (n/2 copies of n/2, n/2-1 copies of n/2-1, and one copy of 1), and the odd-n case leverages a uniform configuration. The general circumference scaling adds another layer of parameterization while preserving difficulty.
notes: Proof sketch: Model the circle as vertices 0,1,...,n-1 equally spaced on a regular n-gon, and a labeling corresponds to a cyclic permutation p(1),...,p(n). Each hop uses the shorter arc, i.e., a step-length d_i := min(|p(i+1)-p(i)|, n - |p(i+1)-p(i)|) in {1,2,...,floor(n/2)}. Let f(x) = x^power with power >= 2 (convex and increasing). The goal is to maximize sum f(d_i). Odd n: Set p(i) = i-1 shifted mod n and alternate direction to ensure each hop is exactly (n-1)/2 steps; all d_i equal k = (n-1)/2. This vector of step-lengths majorizes any other feasible vector because every component is maximal and the cyclic closure constraints permit it; thus by Karamata, the sum f(d_i) is maximized at n * f(k). Even n: One cannot have all d_i = n/2, because the direction parity and cycle closure force a non-diameter correction. A constructive optimal permutation is p = (0, n/2, 1, n/2+1, 2, n/2+2, ..., n/2-1, n-1), returning to 0. Its hop multiset is: n/2 arcs of length n/2 (between i and i+n/2), n/2-1 arcs of length n/2-1 (between n/2+j and j+1 for j=0,...,n/2-2), and one arc of length 1 (from n-1 to 0). To see optimality, sort any feasible d-vector in nonincreasing order and compare partial sums: there can be at most n/2 diameter-length arcs (these must alternate between antipodal halves), at most n/2-1 arcs of length n/2-1 due to adjacency constraints within each half, and necessarily at least one unit-length arc to close the cycle. Thus the sorted optimal d-vector v majorizes any other feasible vector, so sum f(d_i) <= sum f(v_i) by Karamata. Scaling by unit = circumference/n converts steps to actual arc lengths, and raising to power preserves convexity; hence the maximal value is unit^power times the step-count result above. This establishes correctness for all instances generated.
source_question: There are 1038 equally spaced points on a circular track \(\gamma\) of circumference 1038. The points are labeled \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{1038}\) in some order, each label used once. Initially, Bunbun the Bunny begins at \(A_1\). She hops along \(\gamma\) from \(A_1\) to \(A_2\), then from \(A_2\) to \(A_3\), until she reaches \(A_{1038}\), after which she hops back to \(A_1\). When hopping from \(P\) to \(Q\), she always hops along the shorter of the two arcs \(\hat{PQ}\) of \(\gamma\); if \(\bar{PQ}\) is a diameter of \(\gamma\), she moves along either semicircle. Determine the maximal possible sum of the lengths of the 1038 arcs which Bunbun traveled, over all possible labellings of the 1038 points.
